lessons.title: Trace an authenticated request through the Java stack
lessons.overview: Read Auth as a request pipeline, not as a collection of classes. A client request enters a controller, the security filter verifies the Craves access token and creates CurrentUser, authorization decides whether the principal may perform the operation, and the service/repository layer owns the state change. When extending Auth, keep identity derivation on the server and preserve the distinction between authentication, authorization and business validation.

steps.label: Start at the route
steps.detail: Open AuthController and identify the exact HTTP method, path, request DTO and response type before changing implementation code.

steps.label: Follow security
steps.detail: Trace the Bearer token through CravesJwtAuthenticationFilter into CurrentUser; never replace verified identity with a browser-supplied identityId.

steps.label: Follow the service
steps.detail: Locate the service method called by the controller and identify its transaction, validation and repository dependencies.

steps.label: Follow persistence
steps.detail: Identify the owned tables or repository calls and any token-version or role state that can change the result.

steps.label: Map failure responses
steps.detail: Write down the expected unauthenticated, forbidden, validation and dependency-failure outcomes before coding.

lessons.example: For a new administrator-only read endpoint, the controller may expose the route, but CurrentUser and an explicit internal role check remain the authority. Hiding the button in Next.js is only presentation.
lessons.lab: Choose one existing AuthController operation and draw route → security filter → CurrentUser → service → repository. Record the exact classes and one failure at each boundary using only test data.
lessons.pitfall: Do not copy Firebase or JWT claims from the browser into a trusted DTO and treat them as authenticated facts.

questions.prompt: Where should a protected controller obtain the caller identity?
questions.explanation: The verified server-side principal is the authentication boundary.

questions.prompt: What should be mapped before implementing a new protected route?
options: Route, security, service, persistence and failures
questions.explanation: End-to-end ownership prevents security and persistence gaps.

lessons.title: Build a new protected Auth feature without weakening trust
lessons.overview: A safe Auth feature is implemented vertically. Define the API contract, validate input, reuse CurrentUser, place business behavior in a service, persist through the existing repository pattern, and add explicit role checks when the action is internal. If schema changes are required, use a forward database migration rather than runtime table creation. Keep secrets and provider credentials in runtime configuration, never in source or Academy examples.

steps.label: Define contract
steps.detail: Write the request/response shape, status codes and authorization rule before the controller method.

steps.label: Add service behavior
steps.detail: Put state transition and reusable validation in the service layer; keep the controller focused on HTTP concerns.

steps.label: Persist deliberately
steps.detail: Use the existing repository and migration conventions; define uniqueness and concurrency behavior when the operation can be retried.

steps.label: Authorize server-side
steps.detail: Use explicit internal-role checks for administrator actions and verify ownership for customer-scoped actions.

steps.label: Wire the client last
steps.detail: Only after the backend contract is tested should the Next.js BFF or UI call the new route.

steps.label: Document rollback
steps.detail: State how to disable or revert the feature without deleting historical identity or audit data.

lessons.example: If Product approves a new administrator read capability, add the backend endpoint and role boundary first, test 401/403/200 behavior, then expose it through the admin BFF. Do not make an admin page call an unrestricted internal repository directly.
lessons.lab: Design a synthetic administrator read feature. List the Java files you would change, the role required, request/response DTOs, tests and rollback. Do not create a new commercial or customer policy in the exercise.
lessons.pitfall: Do not create a broad role such as any string ending in ADMIN. Reuse the explicit Craves internal-role model or obtain an approved new role design.

questions.prompt: Where should reusable state-changing Auth behavior live?
options: Only in a React click handler
In the service layer behind an authorized controller
questions.explanation: The service layer is the reusable transactional business boundary.

questions.prompt: What should happen before exposing a new admin action in the UI?
questions.explanation: The backend security boundary must exist before the presentation layer.

lessons.title: Test, release and recover an identity change
lessons.overview: Identity changes need negative tests as much as happy-path tests. Validate missing credentials, malformed credentials, wrong roles, stale token versions, invalid payloads and retries. A green build proves code checks passed; release evidence additionally requires the intended artifact, configuration, database migration when applicable, healthy runtime and authenticated smoke tests. Recovery should fail closed rather than granting broader access when a dependency is unavailable.

steps.label: Test denial
steps.detail: Cover 401 and 403 behavior plus malformed or stale authentication inputs.

steps.label: Test success
steps.detail: Use a synthetic authorized principal and assert the precise response and persisted result.

steps.label: Test retries
steps.detail: Verify duplicate calls cannot create unintended duplicate identity state or privilege.

steps.label: Verify configuration
steps.detail: Confirm environment variables and secret references exist in the target environment without copying secret values into evidence.

steps.label: Smoke the deployed route
steps.detail: Run one authorized and one denied request against the intended deployed revision.

steps.label: Recover safely
steps.detail: Prefer disabling the new capability or reverting the compatible code path; never bypass verification to restore availability.

lessons.example: If a deployment causes administrator requests to fail, the recovery action is not to temporarily trust an X-Admin header. Roll back or disable the affected route while preserving verified authentication.
lessons.lab: Create a release checklist for a synthetic Auth change with source SHA, CI result, migration, configuration, authorized smoke, denied smoke and rollback command owner. Use no real tokens or secrets.
lessons.pitfall: Availability pressure is not a reason to introduce an authentication bypass.

questions.prompt: Which smoke test pair best validates a protected Auth route?
questions.explanation: Positive and negative authorization evidence are both required.

questions.prompt: What is the safe response if verification is unavailable after release?
questions.explanation: Identity systems must not trade verification for availability.
